question: Does the gap vs the promise explain score better than raw delivery days?
key_number: Model fit (AIC): gap 209,802 vs speed 211,055, so gap is better by about 1,253 points
caveat: Part of the gap effect reflects survey timing (see next row)

question: Same comparison, only reviews written after the parcel arrived
key_number: Model fit (AIC): speed 197,793 vs gap 198,466, so speed is better by about 673 points; both still add information (p<0.001)
caveat: n = 91,171. Once the parcel has arrived, raw speed explains slightly more than the gap

question: Does each late day cost more than each early day gains?
key_number: Stars per day: late costs 0.122 vs early gains 0.024 (about 5x); after delivery 0.085 vs 0.013 (about 6.5x)
caveat: Size depends on the cap: after delivery the ratio runs from 1.2x (7-day cap) to 7.0x (60-day cap). The late curve flattens after about 8 days

question: Does the same lateness hurt more when the promise was short?
key_number: Late x promise effect per promised day: +0.0026 (all reviews), +0.0014 (timing control), -0.0003 with p=0.81 (after delivery)
caveat: Short-promise orders are reviewed before delivery less often (19.9% vs 25.8% at 1-3 days late), which probably drives the raw pattern

question: Do customers react differently to seller-stage and carrier-stage delay?
key_number: Stars per day: seller stage -0.070 vs carrier stage -0.047 (all reviews); -0.057 vs -0.030 after delivery (p=0.019)
caveat: Only 22.3% of late orders have any seller-stage delay. Handover = carrier pickup minus latest shipping limit date

question: Does non-response bias the results?
key_number: Late orders are less likely to be reviewed (odds ratio 0.25, CI 0.21-0.31), but worst-case bounds on the late-minus-on-time gap are -2.05 to -1.94 vs -2.02 observed
caveat: Review timing (answering before delivery) is the bigger selection issue. Inverse-probability weights leave H2 unchanged
